Gunung Sundoro, in central Java, is located between the Dieng complex to the NW and Sumbing volcano to the SE. The large Kembang cone is about 2.5 km from the summit on the SW flank.
Gunung Sumbing is a stratovolcano that is the SE-most edifice of a chain of volcanoes in central Java that includes Sundoro and the Dieng Complex.
Gunung Merbabu is a massive forested volcano north of Merapi in central Java.
Merapi, one of Indonesia's most active volcanoes, lies in one of the world's most densely populated areas and dominates the landscape immediately north of the major city of Yogyakarta.
The Lawu volcanic complex includes a deeply eroded volcano to the south joined to a younger edifice to the north considered by van Bemmelen (1949b) to be probably Holocene.
The broad Kawi-Butak volcanic massif lies immediately E of Kelut volcano and S of Arjuno-Welirang volcano.
The relatively inconspicuous Kelud stratovolcano contains a summit crater lake that has been the source of some of Indonesia's most deadly eruptions.
Gunung Penanggungan, one of Java's most revered mountains, is a small stratovolcano immediately north of the Arjuno-Welirang massif.
The Arjuno and Welirang volcanoes anchor the SE and NW ends, respectively, of a 6-km-long line of volcanic cones and craters.
Semeru, the highest volcano on Java, and one of its most active, lies at the southern end of a volcanic massif extending north to the Tengger caldera.
The 16-km-wide Tengger caldera is located at the northern end of a volcanic massif extending from Semeru volcano.
Lamongan, a small stratovolcano located between the massive Tengger and Iyang-Argapura volcanic complexes, is surrounded by numerous maars and cinder cones.
The massive Iyang-Argapura volcanic complex dominates the landscape between Raung and Lamongan volcanoes in eastern Java.
Raung, one of Java's most active volcanoes, is a massive stratovolcano in easternmost Java that was constructed SW of the rim of Ijen caldera.
The small andesitic Baluran, dwarfed by its neighbor Ijen volcano to the SW, occupies the very NE tip of Java.
The Ijen volcano complex at the eastern end of Java consists of a group of small stratovolcanoes constructed within the 20-km-wide Ijen (Kendeng) caldera.
The most obvious feature of the Buyan-Bratan volcanic complex in north-central Bali is the 11 x 6 km wide Bratan caldera (also known as Catur or Tjatur caldera), which contains three caldera lakes.
The historically active Batur is located at the center of two concentric calderas NW of Agung volcano.
Symmetrical Agung stratovolcano, Bali's highest and most sacred mountain, towers over the eastern end of the island.
Rinjani volcano on the island of Lombok rises to 3726 m, second in height among Indonesian volcanoes only to Sumatra's Kerinci volcano.
The massive Tambora stratovolcano forms the entire 60-km-wide Sanggar Peninsula on northern Sumbawa Island.
Sangeang Api volcano, one of the most active in the Lesser Sunda Islands, forms a small 13-km-wide island off the NE coast of Sumbawa Island.
The Wai Sano composite volcano at the western end of Flores Island includes a 2.5 x 3.5 km elliptical caldera in the NW part of a larger 9-10 km edifice.
The Anak Ranakah (Child of Ranakah) lava dome was formed in 1987 in an area without previous recorded eruptions at the base of the large older lava dome of Gunung Ranakah.
The symmetrical Gunung Inierie stratovolcano in south-central Flores overlooks the Sawu Sea, and is the highest volcano on the island.
Inielika is a broad, low volcano in central Flores Island that was constructed within the Lobobutu caldera.
Ebulobo, also referred to as Amburombu or Keo Peak, is a steep-sided symmetrical stratovolcano in central Flores Island.
Gunung Iya is the southernmost of a group of three volcanoes comprising a small peninsula south of the city of Ende on central Flores Island.
Kelimutu is a small, but well-known, Indonesian compound volcano in central Flores Island with three summit crater lakes of varying colors.
Paluweh, also known as Rokatenda, forms the 8-km-wide island of Palu'e north of the volcanic arc that cuts across Flores Island.
Gunung Egon, also known as Namang, sits within the narrow section of eastern Flores Island.
The Lewotobi edifice in eastern Flores Island is composed of the two adjacent Lewotobi Laki-laki and Lewotobi Perempuan stratovolcanoes (the "husband and wife").
Iliboleng stratovolcano was constructed at the SE end of Adonara Island across a narrow strait from Lomblen Island.
The Lewotolok (or Lewotolo) stratovolcano occupies the eastern end of an elongated peninsula extending north into the Flores Sea, connected to Lembata (formerly Lomblen) Island by a narrow isthmus.
Ililabalekan volcano is situated on a prominent peninsula in SW Lembata (formerly Lomblen) Island.
Constructed on the southern rim of the Lerek caldera, Iliwerung forms a prominent south-facing peninsula on Lembata (formerly Lomblen) Island.
The small isolated island of Batu Tara is located in the Flores Sea ~50 km N of Lembata (formerly Lomblen) Island and the main volcanic arc.
Sirung is located at the NE end of a volcanic massif with multiple centers that extends 14 km NE from the southern end of Pantar Island.
The andesitic Wurlali stratovolcano was constructed at the northern end of a 5-km-wide caldera on the eastern side of Damar Island in the Banda Sea.
Teon, an elongated andesitic island volcano in the southwestern Banda arc, is also known as Serawerna, the name of its active crater.
The 5 x 6 km Nila Island in the Banda Sea is comprised of a low-rimmed caldera breached at sea level on the south and east, with a youthful forested cone.
The 2 x 4 km island of Serua is the emergent summit of a volcano rising 3,600 m above the Banda Sea floor.
The small steep-sided island of Manuk is the easternmost volcano in the Banda volcanic arc.
The 3-km-wide island of Banda Api is the northern-most volcano in the Banda arc and has a long period of recorded observation because of its key location in the Portuguese and Dutch spice trade.
Colo volcano forms the isolated small island of Una Una in the middle of the Gulf of Tomini in northern Sulawesi.
The compound Ambang volcano is the westernmost of the active volcanoes on the northern arm of Sulawesi.
The Soputan stratovolcano on the southern rim of the Quaternary Tondano caldera on the northern arm of Sulawesi Island is one of Sulawesi's most active volcanoes.
The Lokong-Empung volcanic complex, rising above the plain of Tondano in North Sulawesi, includes four peaks and an active crater.
The elongated Mahawu volcano immediately east of Lokon-Empung volcano is the northernmost of a series of young volcanoes along a SSW-NNE line near the margin of the Quaternary Tondano caldera.
Klabat is a symmetrical stratovolcano near the tip of the northern arm of Sulawesi Island, east of the city of Manado.
The eastern peninsula at the far NE end of Sulawesi near the city of Bitung is occupied by a volcanic complex consisting of two major edifices within a nature reserve.
Ruang volcano is the southernmost volcano in the Sangihe Island arc, north of Sulawesi Island; it is not the better known Raung volcano on Java.
Karangetang (Api Siau) volcano lies at the northern end of the island of Siau, about 125 km NNE of the NE-most point of Sulawesi.
The submarine Banua Wuhu volcanic cone lies ~600 m off the western coast of Mahengatang Island, the emergent summit of a large submarine edifice, in the Sangihe Islands.
The massive Gunung Awu stratovolcano occupies the northern end of Great Sangihe Island, the largest of the Sangihe arc.
Two cinder cones between Galela Bay and Lake Galela on norther Halmahera, NE of Dukono volcano, were mapped by Supriatna (1980) as basaltic and Holocene.
The Dukono complex in northern Halmahera is on an edifice with a broad, low profile containing multiple peaks and overlapping craters.
Gunung Tobaru, also known as Lolodai, is located in northern Halmahera WSW of Dukono and NNE of Ibu.
The truncated summit of Gunung Ibu stratovolcano along the NW coast of Halmahera Island has large nested summit craters.
The shifting of eruption centers on Gamkonora, the highest peak of Halmahera, has produced an elongated series of summit craters along a N-S trending rift.
The Jailolo volcanic complex forms a peninsula west of Jailolo Bay on the western coast of Halmahera Island.
Hiri is a 3-km-wide forested island immediately north of Gamalama on Ternate Island, and is the northernmost of a chain of volcanic islands off the western coast of Halmahera.
Todoko-Ranu is a large volcanic complex south of Gamkonora in North Maluku, Halmahera, that includes two calderas.
The conical Kie Matubu volcano on the south end of Tidore Island is the highest peak of the North Maluku island chain west of Halmahera.
The small volcanic island of Mare, immediately south of Tidore, was mapped as Holocene in age by Apandi and Sudana (1980).
The 5-km-wide island of Moti, also known as Motir, is part of a chain of volcanic islands off the western coast of Halmahera.
Gamalama is a near-conical stratovolcano that comprises the entire island of Ternate off the western coast of Halmahera, and is one of Indonesia's most active volcanoes.
Kie Besi volcano, forming the 10-km-wide Makian island off the west coast of Halmahera, has been the source of infrequent, but strong eruptions that have devastated villages on the island.
Mélébingóy (previously known as Parker) is a low, vegetated stratovolcano overlooking Sarangani Bay near the southern tip of Mindanao Island.
The symmetrical Matutum stratovolcano overlooks the  city of General Santos in southern Mindanao, NW of Sarangani Bay, Philippines.
An andesitic-to-dacitic stratovolcano complex in the Leonard Range is truncated by a 4 x 5 km caldera partially filled by Lake Leonard.

Mount Makaturing is the central edifice in the Butig Mountains S of Lake Lanao in central Mindanao that includes a complex of volcanic cones and craters stretching 10 km E and 15 km WSW. Eruptions at one time…
The large Ragang stratovolcano, also called Piapayungan, is SE of Lake Lanao in central Mindanao.
Musuan, also known as Calayo, is an isolated, low grass-covered andesitic-to-dacitic lava dome and tuff cone that rises above flat farmland in the province of Bukidnon in central Mindanao.
The 20-km-long Camiguin Island just off the coast of north-central Mindanao Island consists of four overlapping stratovolcanoes overlying older buried edifices.
Kanlaon volcano (also spelled Canlaon) forms the highest point on the Philippine island of Negros.
Mount Cabalían, at the SE tip of Leyte Island, is dissected by steep radial ridges that are moderately to thickly vegetated.
The volcanic island of Biliran, located across the narrow Biliran Strait from the northern tip of Leyte Island, contains many prominent andesitic lava domes, the highest of which is 1301 m Surio.
Luzon's southernmost volcano, Bulusan, was constructed along the rim of the 11-km-diameter dacitic-to-rhyolitic Irosin caldera, which was formed about 36,000 years ago.
Symmetrical Mayon, which rises above the Albay Gulf NW of Legazpi City, is the most active volcano of the Philippines.
Mount Iriga (locally known as Mt Asog) is a small andesitic stratovolcano that rises immediately W of Lake Buhi which has satellitic cinder cones of basaltic composition.
The broad isthmus between Lagonoy Gulf and San Miguel Bay in SE Luzon is occupied by Mount Isarog.

Banahaw (also known as Banahao), the highest of a group of volcanoes south and east of Manila, is flanked by San Cristobal (7 km W) and Banahaw de Lucban on the NE. Andesitic-to-dacitic lava domes occur on the flanks…
The San Pablo Volcanic Field, (also known as the Laguna Volcanic Field) lies at the southern end of Laguna de Bay, the largest lake on Luzon Island.
Taal is one of the most active volcanoes in the Philippines and has produced some powerful eruptions.
Prior to 1991 Pinatubo volcano was a relatively unknown, heavily forested lava dome complex located 100 km NW of Manila with no recorded eruptions.
The Mount Cagua stratovolcano lies at the NE tip of Luzon.
Forested Mount Camiguin occupies the SW tip of 22-km-long Camiguin Island in the Babuyan archipelago, north of Luzon Island.
Didicas, 22 km NE of Camiguin Island in the Babuyanes Islands north of Luzon, was a submarine volcano prior to 1952, when a permanent island was formed.
Multiple Quaternary volcanic centers occupy Babuyan de Claro Island north of Luzon.
The morphologically youthful Iraya stratovolcano is the northernmost active volcano in the Philippines.
The Hainan volcanic field consists of Quaternary lava flows that extend over about 4,100 km2 of northern Hainan Island (also known as Qiong).
The Lý Son (formerly known as Cù-Lao Ré) volcanic group consists of four subaerial and nine submarine cones about 150 km off the coast of central Vietnam.

The Ile des Cendres group of submarine volcanoes off the SE coast of Vietnam includes two submarine cones that built ephemeral islands during an eruption in 1923 and two submarine lava cones of uncertain age.
Mount Popa, in central Burma (Myanmar), is a large, steep-sided composite cone that rises above a surrounding lava plateau.
The Tengchong volcanic field, located in southern China near the border with Burma (Myanmar), was active during five periods ranging from the early Pliocene to the Holocene.

Kueishantao Island, the southernmost of five small volcanic islands off the NE coast of Taiwan, is also known as Guieshan Island and "Turtle Mountain Island" due to its profile as seen from some points on Taiwan.
The Tatun (Datun) group consists predominately of a series of andesitic lava domes in the northernmost part of Taiwan.

The southernmost Ryukyu Islands volcano is a shallow submarine volcano 20 km NNE of Iriomotejima island and 35 km WSW of the northern tip of the island of Ishigakishima in an area with an estimated depth of 200-300 m.
Yokoatejima is a 3.5-km-long island NW of Amami Oshima Island at the SW end of the Tokara island chain.
Akusekijima is a small stratovolcano in the southern Ryukyu Islands.
The 1 x 2.7 km island of Io-Torishima, located north of the largest island of the Ryukyus, Okinawa, is composed of two andesitic volcanoes.
The 8-km-long island of Suwanosejima in the northern Ryukyu Islands consists of an andesitic stratovolcano with two active summit craters.

Kuchinoshima, lying in the northern Ryukyu Islands between the volcanic islands of Nakanoshima and Kuchinoerabujima, consists of two andesitic stratovolcanoes and a NW-SE-trending chain of lava domes.
The 9 x 5 km island of Nakanoshima is surrounded by coral reefs.
A group of young stratovolcanoes forms the eastern end of the irregularly shaped island of Kuchinoerabujima in the northern Ryukyu Islands, 15 km W of Yakushima.
Multiple eruption centers have exhibited recent activity at Kikai, a mostly submerged, 19-km-wide caldera near the northern end of the Ryukyu Islands south of Kyushu.

The submerged 15 x 25 km Ata caldera under Kagoshima Bay is one of several large calderas in southern Kyushu and the source of major pyroclastic flows associated with its formation more than 40,000 years ago.
Yonemaru and Sumiyoshiike are basaltic maars formed in coastal lowland deposits north of the Aira caldera, on the SW and SE flanks of the small Pleistocene Aojiki cone.
The Aira caldera in the northern half of Kagoshima Bay contains the post-caldera Sakurajima volcano, one of Japan's most active.
A group of small olivine basaltic shield volcanoes and cinder cones lies at the eastern end of Fukuejima in the Goto Islands off the western coast of Kyushu.
Kirishimayama is a large group of more than 20 Quaternary volcanoes located north of Kagoshima Bay.
The massive Unzendake volcanic complex comprises much of the Shimabara Peninsula east of the city of Nagasaki.
The 24-km-wide Asosan caldera was formed during four major explosive eruptions from 300,000 to 90,000 years ago.
Kujusan is a complex of stratovolcanoes and lava domes lying NE of Aso caldera in north-central Kyushu.
A group of lava domes rises above the hot spring resort city of Beppu on Japan's Inland Sea, possibly within an ancient breached caldera.

The dominantly Pleistocene Abu volcano group, located along northern coast near the SW end of Honshu, consists of basaltic-to-dacitic lava flows, small shield volcanoes (some with associated cinder cones), and lava domes.
Sanbesan stratovolcano, near the northern coast of SW Honshu, has a summit cut by a small caldera about 1 km in diameter.
The Izu-Tobu (or Higashi-Izu) volcano group is scattered over a broad, plateau-like area of more than 400 km2 on the E side of the Izu Peninsula.
Hakoneyama volcano is truncated by two overlapping calderas, the largest of which is 10 x 11 km wide.

The Yokodake lava dome, with eight small craters, is at the northern edge of the Kita-Yatsugatake (North Yatsugatake) group of stratovolcanoes and lava domes at the NW end of the NNW-SSE-trending Yatsugatake volcanic…
The conical form of Fujisan, Japan's highest and most noted volcano, belies its complex origin.
The massive Ontakesan stratovolcano, the second highest volcano in Japan, lies at the southern end of the Northern Japan Alps.
Hakusan is a complex andesitic-dacitic stratovolcano near the western coast of central Honshu.
Norikuradake volcano consists of an elongated group of small andesitic stratovolcanoes and craters arranged along a N-S line above a ridge crest in the southern part of the Northern Japan Alps.
Yakedake rises above the popular resort of Kamikochi in the Northern Japan Alps.
Midagahara volcano is a dissected andesitic-to-dacitic stratovolcano on a plateau surrounded by high peaks of the North Japan Alps.
Niigata-Yakeyama, one of several Japanese volcanoes named Yakeyama ("Burning Mountain"), is an andesitic-to-dacitic lava dome in Niigata prefecture in west-central Honshu, about 20 km from the coast.
Myokosan is a steep-sided basaltic-to-dacitic stratovolcano north of Nagano City that overlooks Lake Nojiri below its SE flank.
Asamayama, Honshu's most active volcano, overlooks the resort town of Karuizawa, 140 km NW of Tokyo.
The Shiga volcanic complex immediately north of Kusatsu-Shirane volcano consists of a group of small andesitic shield volcanoes and pyroclastic cones.
Harunasan is truncated by a small summit caldera containing the symmetrical post-caldera pyroclastic cone of Haruna-Fuji.
The Kusatsu-Shiranesan complex, located immediately north of Asama volcano, consists of a series of overlapping pyroclastic cones and three crater lakes.
Hiuchigatake volcano lies in Nikko National Park and erupted the 8 km3 Hiuchigatake-Nanairi tephra and pyroclastic flow deposit about 170,000-160,000 years ago.
The broad, low dominantly andesitic Akagisan volcano rises above the northern end of the Kanto Plain.
Nantaisan stratovolcano rises above the north shore of Lake Chuzenji in Nikko National Park.
The Omanago volcano group consists of a series of five closely spaced lava domes that were constructed north and NW of Nantai volcano in Nikko National Park.
Takaharayama is a small stratovolcano with lava domes located SW of Nasudake volcano and NNW of Utsunomiya city in central Honshu.

Nikko-Shiranesan is a relatively small, 2578-m-high andesitic volcano consisting of a group of four lava domes resting on a shield volcano that rises to the NW of scenic Lake Chuzenji in Nikko National Park.
Numazawa is a small, 2-km-wide dominantly dacitic-to-rhyolitic caldera constructed within an older Pliocene caldera.
The Nasudake volcanic group consists of a N-S-trending cluster of stratovolcanoes and lava domes at the north end of the Kanto Plain.
One of Japan's most noted volcanoes, Bandaisan rises above the north shore of Lake Inawashiro.
The broad forested massif of Adatarayama volcano is located E of Bandai volcano, about 15 km SW of Fukushima city.
The Azumayama volcanic group consists of a cluster of stratovolcanoes, shield volcanoes, lava domes, and pyroclastic cones.
Hijiori caldera is a small, inconspicuous caldera located NE of the Pleistocene Gassan stratovolcano.
The Zaozan (or Zaosan) volcano group consists of a complex cluster of stratovolcanoes in north-central Honshu about 40 km W of Sendai Bay.
Naruko is a poorly defined, 5.5 x 7 km caldera NW of the city of Sendai.
The summit of Kurikomayama is cut by a 4-km-wide caldera breached to the north that is partially filled by the Tsurugidake central cone, once mined for sulfur.
Chokaisan is composed of two overlapping stratovolcanoes with a conical profile that inspired the local names of Akita-Fuji or Dewa-Fuji.
Two calderas partially filled by basaltic cones cut the summit of Akita-Komagatake volcano.
Viewed from the east, Iwatesan volcano has a symmetrical profile that invites comparison with Fuji, but on the west an older cone is visible containing an oval-shaped, 1.8 x 3 km caldera.
Hachimantai was constructed from widely scattered vents during the Pleistocene and is capped with andesitic lavas from vents in the center of the complex.
Megata, a group of three small maars along the tip of the Oga Peninsula in NW Honshu, has been active during the Holocene (Ishikawa et al., 1957).

One of several Japanese volcanoes named Yakeyama ("Burning Mountain"), Akita-Yakeyama is the most recently active of a group of coalescing edifices in NW Honshu immediately west of Hachimantai volcano.
The lake-filled, 11-km-wide, Towada caldera in northern Honshu formed during as many as six major explosive eruptions over a 40,000-year period ending about 13,000 years ago.
Iwakisan volcano, symmetrical on all but its western flanks, has a 2-km-wide summit crater filled by a lava dome flanked by six explosion craters.
The Hakkodasan complex includes at least 17 stratovolcanoes and lava domes south of Mutsu Bay at the northern end of Honshu.
Osorezan, on the Shimokita Peninsula in northernmost Honshu, contains a 5-km-wide caldera partly occupied by a shallow lake that drains through the N caldera wall.
The small 2 x 2.4 km island of Toshima is located in the northern Izu Islands south of Izu-Oshima Island about 20 km W of the main volcanic front.
Izu-Oshima volcano in Sagami Bay, east of the Izu Peninsula, is the northernmost of the Izu Islands.
The elongated island of Niijima, SSW of Oshima, is 11 km long and only 2.5 km wide.
A cluster of rhyolitic lava domes and associated pyroclastic deposits form the 4 x 6 km island of Kozushima in the northern Izu Islands.
Mikurajima is a small steep-sided island located between the more well-known Miyakejima and Hachijojima volcanoes.
Kurose Hole, between Mikura and Hachijo-jima islands, is a nearly circular submarine caldera 5-7 km in diameter with a 600-760 m deep floor.
The circular, 8-km-wide island of Miyakejima forms a low-angle stratovolcano that rises about 1,100 m from the sea floor in the northern Izu Islands about 200 km SSW of Tokyo.
Hachijojima, in the central Izu Islands about 300 km S of Tokyo, consists of two small Quaternary dominantly basaltic stratovolcanoes forming an elongated NW-SE-trending island.

The large submarine Kita-Bayonnaise (North Bayonnaise) submarine caldera, also known as Myojin Knoll, lies between the Aogashima and Myojinsho (also called Beyonesu Rocks) calderas about 300 km SSE of the Izu Peninsula.
The small 2.5 x 3.5 km dominantly basaltic island of Aogashima is surrounded by steep cliffs and contains a small 1.7 x 1.5-km-wide caldera.
Beyonesu Rocks are part of the barely exposed rim of the largely submarine Myojinsho caldera.
Sumisujima (also known as Smith Rocks) is a steep-sided basaltic pinnacle that forms part of the outer southern flank of a 8-9 km submarine caldera that truncates a 20-km-wide seamount.
Sofugan is a steep-sided pinnacle that rises 99 m above the sea surface south of Torishima volcano.
Suiyo, one of the Shichiyo Seamounts, named for the seven days of the week, lies south of Sofugan volcano.
Mokuyo is one of the Shichiyo Seamounts, named for the seven days of the week.
Doyo is the southernmost of the Shichiyo Seamounts, named for the seven days of the week.
The small island of Nishinoshima was enlarged when several new islands coalesced during an eruption in 1973-74.
Kaikata Seamount is a basaltic-to-dacitic submarine volcano located north of Kaitoku Seamount.
The circular, 2.7-km-wide island of Izu-Torishima in the southern Izu Islands is capped by an unvegetated summit cone formed during an eruption in 1939.
Submarine eruption have been observed during March 1984 and August 2022-January 2023 from Kaitoku Seamount (Kaitoku Kaizan), a three-peaked submarine volcano 80 km NNW of Kita-Ioto.

Eruptions have been recorded since the 18th century from Funka Asane, a submarine edifice ~4 km NW of Kita-Ioto, the northernmost of the Kazan Retto (Volcano Islands), in the southern Ogasawara Volcanic Arc.
Kita-Fukutokutai is a submarine volcano halfway between the Ioto and Minami-Ioto islands.

Ioto, also known as Ogasawara-Iojima to distinguish it from several other "Sulfur Island" volcanoes, lies within a 9-km-wide submarine caldera.The triangular, low-elevation, 8-km-long island narrows toward its SW tip…
Periodic water discoloration and water-spouting have been reported over the Minami-Hiyoshi submarine volcano since 1975, when detonation sounds and an explosion were also reported.
Nikko submarine volcano is a massive seamount that rises from nearly 3 km depth to within 392 m of the ocean surface near the N end of the Mariana Volcanic Arc.
Fukujin seamount in the Mariana Volcanic Arc has risen on occasion to just beneath the ocean surface.
Kasuga 1, the northernmost of three seamounts in the Kasuga seamount chain SE of Fukujin, rises from a depth of 3,000 m to within about 600 m of the ocean surface.
Kasuga 2, also referred to as Minami Kasuga (South Kasuga), is the central of three volcanoes forming the Kasuga seamount chain, which trends SSW from the volcanic front of the Izu-Marianas arc.
NW Eifuku is a small submarine volcano that exhibits vigorous thermal activity.
The conical summit of Daikoku seamount lies along an E-W ridge SE of Eifuku and rises to within 323 m of the sea surface.
Fukutoku-Oka-no-ba is a submarine volcano located 5 km NE of the island of Minami-Ioto.
Ahyi seamount is a large conical submarine volcano ~18 km SE of the island of Farallon de Pajaros in the northern Marianas.
Supply Reef is a conical submarine volcano in the northern Mariana Islands that rises to within 8 m of the surface.
The three small elongated Maug Islands, the largest ~2.3 km long, represent the rim of a 2.5-km-wide caldera on a submarine edifice more than 20 km in diameter.
The small 2-km-wide island of Farallon de Pajaros (also known as Uracas) is the northernmost and most active volcano of the Mariana Islands.
A single large asymmetrical stratovolcano forms 3-km-wide Asuncion Island.
The highest of the Marianas arc volcanoes, Agrigan contains a 500-m-deep, flat-floored caldera.
Pagan Island, the largest and one of the most active of the Mariana Islands volcanoes, consists of two stratovolcanoes connected by a narrow isthmus.
Alamagan is the emergent summit of a large stratovolcano in the central Mariana Islands with a roughly 350-m-deep summit crater east of the center of the island.
Zealandia Bank consists of two pinnacles about 1 km apart rising from a submerged bank to near the ocean surface between Guguan and Sarigan Islands.
Sarigan volcano forms an irregular 3-km-long island consisting of a low truncated cone with a 750-m-wide summit crater that contains a small ash cone.
The island of Guguan, ~2.8 km in diameter, is composed of an eroded volcano on the south, a caldera with a post-caldera cone, and a northern volcano.
The dacitic East Diamante submarine volcano contains an elongated NE-SW-trending caldera with a pronounced rim on the NE side.
Ruby is a basaltic submarine volcano that rises to within about 200 m of the ocean surface near the southern end of the Mariana arc NW of Saipan.
The elongate, 9-km-long island of Anatahan in the central Mariana Islands consists of a large stratovolcano with a 2.3 x 5 km compound summit caldera.
A submarine volcano detected during a 2003 NOAA bathymetric survey of the Mariana Island arc was found to be hydrothermally active and named NW Rota-1.
Esmeralda Bank is a massive submarine volcano with three cones oriented N-S over about 15 km.

Forecast Seamount lies about 70 km W of the southern tip of Guam and about 19 km NW of Seamount X. Hydrothermal fluid temperatures up to 200°C, one of the highest temperature vent systems known in the Mariana arc,…
Hydrothermal activity was detected during a 2003 NOAA expedition at a submarine volcano about 70 km WSW of Guam.
Esan is a small volcanic complex of seven overlapping andesitic-to-dacitic lava domes on the eastern tip of the Oshima Peninsula across the Tsugaru Strait from Honshu.
Oshima-Oshima, a 10 km2 island about 105 km W offshore from the SW tip of Hokkaido, is the emergent summit of two coalescing basaltic-to-andesitic stratovolcanoes.
Much of the truncated Hokkaido-Komagatake andesitic volcano on the Oshima Peninsula of southern Hokkaido is Pleistocene in age.
The Niseko volcano group in SW Hokkaido contains a cluster of andesitic stratovolcanoes and lava domes that extends 25 km E-W and 15 km N-S. The volcanic complex is located NW of Niseko City.
Yoteizan is a symmetrical andesitic-to-dacitic stratovolcano NW of Toya caldera.
The Kuttara volcanic group consists of a series of small stratovolcanoes, lava domes, pyroclastic cones, and a caldera near the Pacific coast SE of Toya caldera and SW of Shikotsu caldera.
Usuzan, one of Hokkaido's most well-known volcanoes, is a small stratovolcano located astride the southern topographic rim of the 110,000-year-old Toya caldera.
Rishirizan is a highly dissected andesitic stratovolcano that forms a 20-km-wide island west of the northern tip of Hokkaido.
The 13 x 15 km Shikotsu caldera, largely filled by the waters of Lake Shikotsu, was formed during one of Hokkaido's largest Quaternary eruptions about 31-34,000 years ago.
Tokachidake volcano consists of a group of dominantly andesitic stratovolcanoes and lava domes arranged on a NE-SW line above a plateau of welded Pleistocene tuffs in central Hokkaido.

The Nipesotsu-Maruyama volcano group, located west of Nukabira Lake about 20 km E of Tokachidake volcano, is composed of a number of overlapping andesitic-to-rhyolitic stratovolcanoes and lava domes constructed along…
The Taisetsuzan volcano group lies at the northern end of the Taisetsu-Tokachi graben in central Hokkaido.
Akan is a 13 x 24 km caldera located immediately SW of Kussharo caldera in eastern Hokkaido.
Mashu is a 6-km-wide Holocene caldera that truncates a stratovolcano constructed on the ESE rim of the large Kussharo caldera.
Rausudake is an andesitic-to-dacitic stratovolcano with summit lava domes on the Shiretoko Peninsula in NE Hokkaido.
The 20 x 26 km Kussharo caldera (also spelled Kutcharo or Kuccharo), is the largest of a cluster of calderas in NE Hokkaido.
Shiretoko-Iozan, one of many Japanese "sulfur mountains," is noted for the extrusion of molten sulfur during eruptions in 1889 and 1936.
Tomariyama, also known as Golovnin, forms the southern end of Kunashir Island, across the Nemuro Strait from Hokkaido.
Ruruidake is a late Pleistocene andesitic-to-dacitic volcanic complex on the NW tip of Kunashir Island in the southern Kuriles, NW of Chachadake [Tiatia} volcano.
Raususan, also known as Mendeleev, is a low compound stratovolcano located in the southern part of Kunashir Island.
The symmetrical Chachadake, also known as Tiatia, is on the SE side of northern Kunashir Island in the southern Kuriles.
The Berutarubesan andesitic-to-dacitic stratovolcano forms the SW tip of Iturup Island in the southern Kuriles.
The conical Etorofu-Atosanupuri stratovolcano forms a peninsula joined to the SW side of Iturup (Etorofu) Island by an isthmus 30 m high.

The Hitokappu Volcano Group [Bogatyr Ridge] on Iturup Island in the southern Kuriles consists of a cluster of late-Pleistocene to Holocene cones and craters extending ~14 km NE-SW. The basaltic andesite to andesitic…
The Etorofu-Yakeyama (Ivan Grozny) complex is located in the center of Iturup Island.
The Sashiusudake (also known as Baransky) volcanic complex along the Pacific coast in the central part of Iturup Island consists of a Holocene stratovolcano built over an eroded Pleistocene edifice.
The Moyorodake volcanic complex (also known as Medvezhia) occupies the NE end of Iturup (Etorofu) Island.
The Ivao group of cones along the Krishtofovich Ridge of SW Urup Island contains several well-preserved cones of Holocene age.
A group of Holocene volcanoes in central Urup Island is named after its most prominent volcano, Kolokol.

A shallow flat-topped edifice ~8 km in diameter, with depths from 0-50 m, is located in the Urup Strait ~15 km S of the Chernyye Brat'ya (Black Brothers) islands and ~20 km ENE of Urup Island in the Kuril Islands.
Chirpoi, a small island lying between the larger islands of Simushir and Urup, contains a half dozen volcanic edifices constructed within an 8-9 km wide, partially submerged caldera.
Milna (or Mil'na) is the southernmost volcano on Simushir Island in the central Kuriles, and includes the Goriaschaia Sopka lava dome on the NW flank.
The Zavaritzki volcano on Simushir Island in the central Kuril Islands contains three nested calderas 10, 8, and 3 km in diameter.
The northernmost volcano on Simushir Island, Uratman consists of a 7.5-km-wide Pleistocene caldera with walls that rise 450 m above a 250-m-deep caldera bay.
Symmetrical Prevo Peak, also known as Simushiru-Fuji for its resemblance to Japan's noted volcano, is capped by a 500 x 600 m summit crater.
The circular 10-km-wide Ketoi island, which rises across the 19-km-wide Diana Strait from Simushir Island, hosts of one of the most complex volcanic structures of the Kuril Islands.
Remnants of the Srednii submarine volcano form a hazardous obstruction in the strait between Rasshua and Ushishur Islands.
The subaerial portion of Ushishur volcano in the central Kuriles is exposed in two small islands, the southern containing the summit caldera and the northern a portion of the volcano's flanks.
The elongated 6 x 13 km island of Rasshua in the central Kuriles contains three overlapping central cones within a 6 km caldera whose eastern margin is beyond the shoreline.
Sarychev Peak, one of the most active volcanoes of the Kuril Islands, occupies the NW end of Matua Island in the central Kuriles.
A low truncated volcano forms the small barren Raikoke Island, which lies 16 km across the Golovnin Strait from Matua Island in the central Kuriles.
The small, mostly unvegetated 3-km-wide island of Chirinkotan occupies the far end of an E-W volcanic chain that extends nearly 50 km W of the central part of the main Kuril Islands arc.
The small 5 x 7.5 km island of Ekarma lies 8.5 km N of Shiashkotan Island along an E-W-trending volcanic chain extending westward from the central part of the main Kuril Island arc.
Sinarka volcano, occupying the northern end of Shiashkotan Island in the central Kuriles, has a complex structure.
The 8 x 12 km island of Kharimkotan (also spelled Harimkotan) in the northern Kuriles consists of a stratovolcano cut by two breached depressions on the east and NW sides.
The southern half of Onekotan Island in the northern Kuril Islands contains the 7.5-km-wide Tao-Rusyr caldera, which is mostly filled by Kal'tsevoe lake.

Nemo Peak volcano at the northern end of Onekotan Island in the northern Kuriles is truncated by two preglacial nested calderas, the largest of which is 10 km in diameter and extends to the northern coast.
The 3-km-diameter island of Shirinki is located west of the main Kuril Island arc and ~20 km WSW of Fuss Peak on Paramushir Island.
Fuss Peak forms a peninsula that lies across a low isthmus on the SW coast of Paramushir Island in the northern Kuriles.
The Karpinsky Group on southern Paramushir Island in the Kuril Islands consists of three Holocene andesitic volcanic centers at the southern end of the Karpinsky Ridge.
Chikurachki, the highest volcano on Paramushir Island in the northern Kuriles, is a relatively small cone constructed on a high Pleistocene edifice.
The Vernadsky Ridge on northern Paramushir island in the northern Kuriles is a large massif with over 40 volcanic centers in three volcano groups each ~7-8 km apart.
The flat-topped summit of the central cone of Ebeko volcano, one of the most active in the Kuril Islands, occupies the northern end of Paramushir Island.
The highest and northernmost volcano of the Kuril Islands, Alaid is a symmetrical stratovolcano when viewed from the north, but has a 1.5-km-wide summit crater that is breached open to the south.

The southernmost major stratovolcano on the Kamchatka peninsula, Kambalny has a summit crater that is breached to the SE. Five Holocene cinder cones on the W and SE flanks have produced fresh-looking lava flows.

Yavinsky is an early to mid-Pleistocene basaltic volcano that forms an arcuate ridge (Yavinsky Khrebet) along the SW coast of Kamchatka, overlooking the town of Ozernovsky and the mouth of the Ozernaya River.
Diky Greben is a lava-dome complex that formed in the center of the 20 x 25 km Pauzhetka caldera, which also contains the Kurile Lake caldera to the east.
Kurile Lake caldera lies within the eastern part of the massive Pauzhetka caldera, but is considered as a separate volcanic system here.
Koshelev is at the southern end of the Kamchatka Peninsula, SW of the Pauzhetka volcano-tectonic depression and NW of Kambalny volcano.

The conical Iliinsky volcano (also spelled Ilyinsky), rising dramatically to 1555 m above the NE shore of Kurile Lake, was constructed beginning about 7600 radiocarbon years ago at the NE margin of Kurile Lake caldera.
Zheltovsky volcano was constructed during the last 8000 years within a 4 x 5 km caldera truncating an earlier Pleistocene edifice.
A large group of Quaternary basaltic pyroclastic cones and associated lava flows (Masurenkov, 1980) fills a topographic low W and NW of Ksudach and Khodutka volcanoes.
Khodutka stratovolcano was formed during the late-Pleistocene to early Holocene, partially covering the older Priemysh stratovolcano on the NW flank.
The Asacha group is a complex massif of Pleistocene-to-Holocene volcanoes located within a distinctly fault-bounded crustal block WSW of Mutnovsky volcano.

The basaltic Visokiy cone is the largest and central feature of a 10-km-long line of basaltic cinder cones between Asacha to the SW and Gorely to the NE. The small Golyi shield volcano lies immediately to the WSW…
Ksudach is unique among Kamchatka volcanoes in its morphology and geologic history.
Massive Mutnovsky, one of the most active volcanoes of southern Kamchatka, is formed of four coalescing stratovolcanoes of predominantly basaltic composition.
Gorely volcano consists of five small overlapping stratovolcanoes constructed along a WNW-ESE line within a large 9 x 13 km caldera.
Tolmachev Dol (Tomachev Plateau) is broad volcanic highland NE of Opala volcano that includes numerous late-Pleistocene and Holocene cinder cones and associated lava flows.
Vilyuchinsky, or Vilyuchik, is a steep-sided Pleistocene-to-Holocene stratovolcano south of Avachinsky Bay.
The Barkhatnaya Sopka group of Pleistocene andesitic-to-rhyolitic lava domes and Holocene basaltic pyroclastic cones is located along the Paratunka River about 30 km NNW of Gorely volcano.
The steep-sided conical Opala stratovolcano was constructed during the late-Pleistocene to Holocene at the northern end of the 12 x 14 km, 40,000-year-old Opala caldera.
The large symmetrical Koryaksky stratovolcano is the most prominent landmark of the NW-trending Avachinskaya volcano group, which towers above Kamchatka's largest city, Petropavlovsk.
Avachinsky, one of Kamchatka's most active volcanoes, rises above Petropavlovsk, Kamchatka's largest city.
Dzenzursky is a strongly eroded stratovolcano of Pleistocene age that lies along a ridge extending NW from Zhupanovsky volcano.
Cinder cones along the Levaya Avacha River about 60 km N of Petropavlovsk-Kamchatskiy erupted lavas over young river terraces.
A group of basaltic cinder cones lies south of Bakening volcano, west of the Srednaya Avacha (Middle Avacha) river valley.
Bakening (also known as Bakenin) lies well west of the eastern volcanic range of Kamchatka, at the head of the Srednyaya Avacha River, about 100 km NNW of Petropavlovsk.

Zavaritsky volcano consists of a complex of six cinder cones trending NW-SE, and an explosion crater located near the headwaters of the Levaya Avacha River west of the main Eastern Kamchatka volcanic arc.
The lake-filled Akademia Nauk caldera is one of three volcanoes constructed within the mid-Pleistocene, 15-km-wide Polovinka caldera.
The Zhupanovsky volcanic massif consists of four overlapping stratovolcanoes along a WNW-trending ridge.
Karymsky is a symmetrical stratovolcano constructed within a 5-km-wide caldera that formed during the early Holocene.
Maly Semyachik is a compound stratovolcano located in a 10-km-wide caldera within the 15 x 20 km mid-Pleistocene Stena-Soboliny caldera.
The Bolshoi Semiachik volcanic complex was constructed within a 10-km-wide caldera whose rim is exposed only on the west.

Taunshits volcano, located west of the massive Uzon caldera, is an andesitic stratovolcano that was constructed beginning about 39,000 years before present (BP) on top of a large Pleistocene tuya pedestal.
The Uzon and Geysernaya calderas, containing Kamchatka's largest geothermal area, form a 7 x 18 km depression that originated during multiple mid-Pleistocene eruptions.

Kikhpinych, the youngest stratovolcano of the Eastern Volcanic Zone of Kamchatka, contains three summits constructed along a roughly E-W line above the eroded Pleistocene Pik volcano, NE of the Uzon caldera.
The late Pleistocene to Holocene Krasheninnikov volcano is comprised of two overlapping stratovolcanoes within a 9 x 10 km Pleistocene caldera.
The symmetrical Kronotsky stratovolcano on the Kamchatka Peninsula lies between the Pacific Ocean and Lake Kronotsky.
Gamchen is a complex volcano composed of four stratovolcanoes, one of which is of Holocene age.

Visoky, at the northern end of a chain of small volcanoes trending NNW from Gamchen volcano, is a small Holocene stratovolcano with a youthful-looking summit crater constructed over the east flank of the Pleistocene…
Komarov volcano is a complex structure along the Gamchen ridge.
Kizimen is an isolated, conical stratovolcano that is morphologically similar to St.
The Udina volcanic massif consists of two conical stratovolcanoes constructed along a WNW-ESE line at the south end of the Kliuchevskaya volcanic group, SE of Tolbachik volcano.
The eroded stratovolcanoes of Ostraya and Ovalnaya Zimina form a ridge north of the Udina complex at the SE end of the Kliuchevskaya volcano group.
The massive Tolbachik volcano is located at the southern end of the Kliuchevskaya volcano group.

The axial crest of Segment J of the Southern East Pacific Rise consists of an asymmetrical shallow graben varying from 250 to 600 m wide with walls about 20 m high.
The narrow axial crest of Segment I of the Southern East Pacific Rise in some places is less than 50 m wide.

Acoustic T-waves from a seismic swarm, possibly associated with magmatic activity, were recorded in 1991 from a location 130 km S of the Eltanin Fracture Zone (Bulletin of the Global Volcanism Network, 1991).

Pinacate is a roughly 55 x 60 km volcanic field in the Sonoran desert of NW México.
Isla San Luis is the largest of the seven Encantada islands at the NW end of the Guaymas lineament in the northern part of the Gulf of California.
The Jaraguay Volcanic Field is the northernmost of a group of large young alkalic volcanic fields in Baja California.
The San Borja (or El Rosarito) volcanic field, is located in central Baja California NE of the Vizcaino Peninsula.
A youthful shield volcano forms Isla Tortuga, which lies in the Gulf of California, 40 km off the Baja coast.
The Comondú-La Purísima volcanic field, located in southern Baja California, west of the Sierra de la Giganta, dates back to the Miocene.

Socorro, the SE-most of the Revillagigedo Islands south of Baja California, is the summit of a massive, predominately submarine basaltic shield volcano capped by a largely buried, 4.5 x 3.8-km-wide summit caldera.
The broad Durango volcanic field covers 2,100 km2 at the NW corner of the Meseta Central near the eastern edge of the Sierra Madre Occidental of north-central México.
Volcán Sangangüey, the highest volcano of the NW-SE-trending Tepic-Zacoalco graben, is an eroded andesitic and dacitic stratovolcano that contains a prominent lava spine at its summit.

Volcán Bárcena, formed by eruptions during 1952-53, is the most prominent feature of the 4.5-km-long Isla San Benedicto, the NE-most of the Revillagigedo Islands, 350 km S of the tip of Baja California.
A group of calc-alkaline andesitic and lamprophyre cinder cones and lava domes, along with associated lava flows, is located near the town of Mascota about 50 km E of Puerto Vallarta.
Volcán Ceboruco is the only volcano in the NW part of the Mexican Volcanic Belt with observed eruptions.
The Colima complex is the most prominent volcanic center of the western Mexican Volcanic Belt.

The Zitácuaro-Valle de Bravo volcanic field in the central part of the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt consists of a broad region of shield volcanoes, lava domes, and cinder cones surrounding the city of Heroica de Zitácuaro.
The composite Jocotitlán volcano, which rises above the Toluca basin 60 km WNW of Mexico City, was constructed during the Pleistocene of andesitic-to-dacitic lava flows.

The widespread Michoacán-Guanajuato volcanic field contains over 1,400 vents, including the historically active cinder cones of Parícutin and Jorullo, covering a 200 x 250 km wide area of Michoacán and Guanajuato…
Nevado de Toluca, México's fourth highest peak, rises above the Toluca basin about 80 km W of Mexico City.
Iztaccíhuatl (the "Woman in White") presents the profile of a sleeping woman as seen from the Valley of Mexico.
The massive Chichinautzin volcanic field extends over an 88 km E-W area immediately south of Mexico City.
La Malinche is an eroded stratovolcano, cut by deep canyons, NE of the city of Puebla.

The Serdán-Oriental Volcanic Field, covering an area 35-40 km E-W and 60 km N-S, includes numerous late Pleistocene to Holocene rhyolitic lava domes, tuff cones, tuff rings, lava flows, and scoria cones.
Los Humeros is the easternmost of a series of silicic volcanic centers with active geothermal systems located north of the axis of the Mexican Volcanic Belt.

The Naolinco Volcanic Field in the Sierra de Chiconquiaco range north of Jalapa (Xalapa), Veracruz, consists of a broad area of scattered Quaternary pyroclastic cones and associated dominantly basaltic lava flows.
Volcán Popocatépetl, whose name is the Aztec word for smoking mountain, rises 70 km SE of Mexico City to form North America's 2nd-highest volcano.

Pico de Orizaba (Volcán Citlaltépetl), México's highest peak and North America's highest volcano, lies at the southern end of a volcanic chain extending north to Cofre de Perote volcano, east of the Serdan-Oriental Basin.
Volcán de San Martín, part of the Tuxtla Volcanic Field, is a broad alkaline shield volcano that rises above the Gulf of Mexico.
El Chichón is a small trachyandesitic tuff cone and lava dome complex in an isolated part of the Chiapas region in SE México.
Tacaná is a 4064-m-high composite stratovolcano that straddles the México/Guatemala border at the NW end of the Central American volcanic belt.
Tajumulco is Guatemala's highest peak and the highest volcano in Central America.
Symmetrical, forest-covered Santa María volcano is part of a chain of large stratovolcanoes that rise above the Pacific coastal plain of Guatemala.
Volcán de Almolonga is an andesitic stratovolcano with a 3.3-km-wide late-Pleistocene central caldera that is located along the Zunil fault zone.
Volcán Atitlán is one of several conical stratovolcanoes in the Guatemalan highlands.
Volcán Tolimán is a large andesitic stratovolcano that rises above the S shore of Lake Atitlán.
Acatenango is ~15 km SW of the city of Antigua, Guatemala, and 3 km N of Fuego volcano.
Volcán Fuego, one of Central America's most active volcanoes, is also one of three large stratovolcanoes overlooking Guatemala's former capital, Antigua.
The symmetrical, forested Volcán de Agua stratovolcano forms an impressive backdrop to the city of Antigua, Guatemala, opposite from the Fuego and Acatenango volcanoes.
The Cuilapa-Barbarena volcanic field contains approximately 70 Quaternary cinder cones, generally less than 100 m high.
Eruptions from Pacaya are frequently visible from Guatemala City, the nation's capital.
Jumaytepeque is a small basaltic stratovolcano located NNE of the city of Cuilapa, north of the major NW-SE-trending Jalpatagua fault that cuts diagonally across SE Guatemala.
Tecuamburro is a small forested stratovolcano, or large lava-dome complex, about 50 km ESE of Guatemala City and 20 km S of the main volcanic chain.
Moyuta is the easternmost of a chain of large stratovolcanoes extending along the volcanic front of Guatemala.
Volcán de Flores is one of the largest of a cluster of small stratovolcanoes located in SE Guatemala behind the volcanic front.
Deeply dissected Volcán Tahual rises ~700 m above plains S of the town of Monjas.
A cluster of cinder cones and low shield volcanoes surrounds the city of Jutiapa in SE Guatemala.
The summit of the andesitic-to-basaltic Volcán Suchitán stratovolcano, NE of the city of Jutiapa, is elongated N-S. Several large canyons cut the slopes of the dominantly andesitic edifice.
Volcán Chingo is a symmetrical stratovolcano that straddles the Guatemala/El Salvador border.
Ixtepeque volcano, which takes its name from the Aztec word for obsidian, is perhaps the largest obsidian field in North America.
The most prominent feature of a volcanic field in the interior valley of El Salvador near the Guatemalan border SE of Volcán Chingo is Cerro Singüil.

The Apaneca Range (also known as the Cuyanausul Range) consists of a group of basaltic-to-andesitic Pleistocene and Holocene stratovolcanoes in western El Salvador between the Santa Ana complex and the Guatemala border.
Santa Ana (also known as Ilamatepec), is a massive, dominantly andesitic-to-trachyandesitic stratovolcano in El Salvador immediately W of Coatepeque Caldera.
Volcán de Izalco began growing in 1770 CE on the southern flank of Santa Ana volcano, eventually building a steep 650-m-high stratovolcano truncated by a 250-m-wide summit crater.
Coatepeque is a 6.5 x 11.5 km collapse caldera ~50 km W of San Salvador that is largely occupied by a lake with hot springs near the margins.

Cerro Cinotepeque is the largest and most prominent of a group of four pyroclastic cones mapped as Holocene by Weber and Weismann (1978) in low-lying areas on either side of the Río Lempa, ~40 km N of San Salvador.
The massive compound San Salvador volcano dominates the landscape W of El Salvador's capital city of San Salvador.
The 8 x 11 km Ilopango caldera, filled by one of El Salvador's largest lakes, has a scalloped 150-500 m high rim.
Taburete volcano rises above the Pacific coastal plain E of the Río Lempa at the SW end of a cluster of volcanoes between San Vincente and San Miguel volcanoes.
San Vicente stratovolcano, also known as Chichontepec, is ~20 km SE of Lake Ilopango.
Usulután volcano anchors the SE end of a cluster of basaltic to basaltic andesite stratovolcanoes between San Vicente and San Miguel volcanoes.
Cerro el Tigre is the highest, NE-most, and oldest of the cluster of coalescing basaltic to basaltic andesite Quaternary volcanoes between the Río Lempa and San Miguel volcano.
Tecapa is a complex basaltic-to-andesitic stratovolcano at the NW end of a cluster of volcanoes E of the Río Lempa between San Vicente and San Miguel volcanoes.
The small Chinameca stratovolcano (also known as El Pacayal) lies across a low saddle about 7 km NW of the large San Miguel volcano.
A solitary, 1-km-wide, lake-filled maar, Laguna Aramuaca, occupies a low-lying area about 10 km SE of the city of San Miguel.
The symmetrical cone of San Miguel, one of the most active volcanoes in El Salvador, rises from near sea level to form one of the country's most prominent landmarks.
Isla del Tigre is a small, 5-km-wide island located across a narrow 2-km-wide strait S of Isla Zacate Grande in the Gulf of Fonseca.
Zacate Grande volcano forms a low island 7 x 10 km wide across a narrow strait from the end of a peninsula surrounded on three sides by the Gulf of Fonseca and Chismuyo bay.
The Lago Yojoa volcanic field consists a group of Pleistocene-to-Holocene scoria cones and collapse pits (Williams and McBirney, 1969).
Cosigüina (also spelled Cosegüina) is a low basaltic-to-andesitic composite volcano that is isolated from other eruptive centers in the Nicaraguan volcanic chain.
The San Cristóbal volcanic complex, consisting of five principal volcanic edifices, forms the NW end of the Marrabios Range.
Telica, one of Nicaragua's most active volcanoes, has erupted frequently since the beginning of the Spanish era.
Nicaragua's youngest volcano, Cerro Negro, was created following an eruption that began in April 1850 about 2 km NW of the summit of Las Pilas volcano.
Las Pilas-El Hoyo volcanic complex, overlooking Cerro Negro volcano to the NW, includes a diverse cluster of cones within about a 3-km-diameter area.
The Apoyeque volcanic complex occupies the broad Chiltepe Peninsula, which extends into south-central Lake Managua.

The Nejapa-Miraflores alignment (also known as Nejapa-Ticoma), ~10 km S of Apoyeque near the western margin of the Nicaraguan graben, cuts through the western part of the capital city of Managua and marks the…
Momotombo is a young stratovolcano that rises prominently above the NW shore of Lake Managua, forming one of Nicaragua's most familiar landmarks.
The Granada lineament, also known as the La Joya alignment, is an arcuate fissure extending from about 2 km SE of the Apoyo caldera rim around to N of the city of Granada.

Masaya volcano in Nicaragua has erupted frequently since the time of the Spanish Conquistadors, when an active lava lake prompted attempts to extract the volcano's molten "gold" until it was found to be basalt rock…
Zapatera is a small low shield volcano that forms a 7 x 10 km wide island on the western side of Lake Nicaragua just offshore from Mombacho volcano.
Mombacho is an andesitic and basaltic stratovolcano on the shores of Lake Nicaragua south of the city of Granada that has undergone edifice collapse on several occasions.

Volcán Concepción is a symmetrical basaltic-to-dacitic stratovolcano that forms the NW half of the dumbbell-shaped island of Ometepe in Lake Nicaragua and is connected to neighboring Madera volcano by a narrow isthmus.
Orosí is one of a cluster of four eroded and vegetated cones in the Guanacaste Range at the NW corner of Costa Rica.
Rincón de la Vieja is a volcanic complex in the Guanacaste Range of NW Costa Rica.
The 225 km2 dominantly andesitic Tenorio volcanic massif anchors the SE end of the Guanacaste Range and consists of a cluster of densely forested NNW-SSE-trending volcanic cones.
Conical Volcán Arenal is the youngest stratovolcano in Costa Rica and one of its most active.
The Platanar volcanic center is the NW-most volcano in the Cordillera Central of Costa Rica.
Miravalles is an andesitic stratovolcano that is one of five post-caldera cones along a NE-trending line within the broad 15 x 20 km Guayabo (Miravalles) caldera.
The broad vegetated edifice of Poás, one of the most active volcanoes of Costa Rica, contains three craters along a N-S line.
One of three massive volcanoes close to the capital city of San José, Volcán Barva (Barba) is a complex volcano with multiple peaks and flank vents.
The massive Irazú volcano in Costa Rica, immediately E of the capital city of San José, covers an area of 500 km2 and is vegetated to within a few hundred meters of its broad summit crater complex.

Turrialba, the easternmost of Costa Rica's Holocene volcanoes, is a large vegetated basaltic-to-dacitic stratovolcano located across a broad saddle NE of Irazú volcano overlooking the city of Cartago.
The westernmost volcano in Panamá, Barú, is a complex dominantly andesitic stratovolcano in the Talamanca Range near the Costa Rica border.
The andesitic-to-dacitic Romeral stratovolcano lies at the northern end of the Ruiz-Tolima volcanic chain, NW of Cerro Bravo volcano, and east of the towns of Neira and Aranzazu.
Cerro Bravo is a relatively low dominantly dacitic lava-dome complex north of Nevado del Ruiz that was constructed within the Pleistocene Quebrada Seca caldera.
Santa Isabel is a small andesitic shield volcano that is dwarfed by its neighbors to the NE (Nevado del Ruiz) and SE (Tolima).
Nevado del Ruiz is a broad, glacier-covered volcano in central Colombia that covers more than 200 km2.
The steep-sided, glacier-covered Nevado del Tolima volcano contrasts with the broad profile of Nevado del Ruiz to the north.

The small Cerro Machín stratovolcano lies at the southern end of the Ruiz-Tolima massif about 20 km WNW of the city of Ibagué. A 3-km-wide caldera is breached to the south and contains three forested dacitic lava domes.
Nevado del Huila, the highest peak in the Colombian Andes, is an elongated N-S-trending volcanic chain mantled by a glacier icecap.
Volcán Sotará, also known as Cerro Azafatudo, is an  andesitic-dacitic stratovolcano about 25 km SSE of Popayán city in southern Colombia, SW of Puracé volcano.
Puracé is an active andesitic volcano with a 600-m-diameter summit crater at the NW end of the Los Coconucos Volcanic Chain.
The forested Doña Juana stratovolcano contains two calderas, breached to the NE and SW. The summit of the andesitic-dacitic volcano is comprised of a series of post-caldera lava domes.
Galeras, a stratovolcano with a large breached caldera located immediately west of the city of Pasto, is one of Colombia's most frequently active volcanoes.
Azufral stratovolcano in southern Colombia, also known as Azufral de Túquerres, is truncated by a 2.5 x 3 km caldera containing a Holocene rhyodacitic lava-dome complex.
Many youthful lava flows extend from the glacier-capped Cumbal volcano, the southernmost historically active volcano of Colombia.
The Chiles-Cerro Negro volcanic complex includes both the Pleistocene Chiles and the Cerro Negro de Mayasquer stratovolcanoes astride the Colombia-Ecuador border.
Volcán el Soche, a small stratovolcano near the Colombia border, is the northernmost of a chain of Ecuadorian volcanoes east of the principal volcanic axis.
The Chachimbiro volcanic complex lies about 25 km NW of the city of Ibarra.
The scenic lake-filled Cuicocha caldera is located at the southern foot of the sharp-peaked Pleistocene Cotacachi stratovolcano about 100 km N of Quito.
Imbabura volcano rises to the north above scenic Laguna de San Pablo in the Interandean valley about 60 km N of Quito.
Mojanda, one of the largest volcanoes of Ecuador's northern Interandean Depression, rises SW of the historic town of Otavalo.
The massive compound andesitic-dacitic Cayambe stratovolcano is located on the western edge of the Cordillera Real, east of the Inter-Andean Valley.
Pululahua is a relatively low, forested volcano about 15 km N of Quito.
Volcán El Reventador is the most frequently active of a chain of Ecuadorian volcanoes in the Cordillera Real, well east of the principal volcanic axis.
Atacazo, located about 25 km SW of Quito, consists of a large Pleistocene andesitic stratovolcanoes truncated by a late-Pleistocene to Holocene caldera.
Chacana is a massive, eroded caldera complex of Pliocene-Holocene age that forms one of the largest rhyolitic centers of the northern Andes.
Guagua Pichincha and the older Pleistocene Rucu Pichincha stratovolcanoes form a broad volcanic massif that rises immediately W of Ecuador's capital city, Quito.
The Aliso volcanic complex lies at the eastern foot of the Ecuadorian Andes, east of Antisana volcano and SW of the town of Baeza.
Antisana is a massive, glacier-covered stratovolcano NE of Cotopaxi, along the western margin of the Eastern Cordillera, 50 km SE of Quito.
The two glacier-covered peaks of Iliniza volcano are prominent landmarks west of the Interandean Valley.
The forested Sumaco stratovolcano rises above the jungles of the western Amazon basin, east of Antisana volcano, and occupies an isolated position far to the east of the main Andes volcanic axis.
The symmetrical, glacier-covered, Cotopaxi stratovolcano is Ecuador's most well-known volcano and one of its most active.

Glacier-clad Chimborazo, Ecuador's highest volcano, anchors the southern end of the country's "Avenue of Volcanoes" 30 km NW of the city of Riobamba.
The Licto group of scoria cones lies along the Río Chambo ~25 km SE of the city of Riobamba and just north of the town of Licto.
Tungurahua, a steep-sided andesitic-dacitic stratovolcano that towers more than 3 km above its northern base, is one of Ecuador's most active volcanoes.
The isolated Sangay volcano, located east of the Andean crest, is the southernmost of Ecuador's volcanoes and its most active.
Volcán Ecuador straddles the equator at the NW end of Isabela Island.
Fernandina, the most active of Galápagos volcanoes and the one closest to the Galápagos mantle plume, is a basaltic shield volcano with a deep 5 x 6.5 km summit caldera.
Volcán Wolf, the highest volcano of the Galápagos Islands, straddles the equator at the north end of the archipelago's largest island, Isabela.
Volcán Darwin, named after the renowned naturalist, contains a symmetrical 5-km-wide, 200-m-deep summit caldera whose floor is nearly covered by youthful lava flows.
Alcedo is one of the lowest and smallest of six shield volcanoes on Isabela Island.
The broad shield volcano of Sierra Negra at the southern end of Isabela Island contains a shallow 7 x 10.5 km caldera that is the largest in the Galápagos Islands.

Located at the SW tip of the J-shaped Isabela Island, Cerro Azul contains a steep-walled 4 x 5 km nested summit caldera complex that is one of the smallest diameter, but at 650 m one of the deepest in the Galápagos…
The elongated island of Pinta is a shield volcano with numerous cones and lava flows originating from NNW-trending fissures.
The small, very low island of Genovesa is the top of a shield volcano.
The low shield volcano forming Marchena Island contains one of the largest calderas of the Galápagos Islands.
The highlands of the broad Santa Cruz shield volcano rise to the N above the Charles Darwin Research Station at Academy Bay.
The elongated shield volcano of Santiago Island, also known as San Salvador Island or James Island, has numerous scattered Holocene pyroclastic cones.
San Cristóbal Island consists of a densely vegetated western part and a lower, younger eastern part with many unvegetated lava flows.
The Quimsachata-Oroscocha group consists of two late Pleistocene and Holocene monogenetic volcanoes at the foot of the Cordillera Oriental, far east of the main volcanic front.
The Cerro Auquihuato cinder cone lies ~30 km NE of Sara Sara volcano.
Nevado Coropuna is a massive ice-covered volcanic complex with multiple summit cones built over a 12 x 20 km area.
The Andahua-Orcopampa volcanic field in the Andahua (or Andagua) valley area, 20 km ENE of Nevados de Coropuna, is a large 60 x 60 km scoria cone and lava field.
The monogenetic Huambo volcanic field lies SSE of the Andahua-Orcocampo volcanic field, west of Sabancaya volcano.
Sabancaya, located in the saddle NE of Ampato and SE of Hualca Hualca volcanoes, is the youngest of these volcanic centers and the only one to have erupted in historical time.
El Misti is a symmetrical andesitic stratovolcano with nested summit craters immediately NE of the city of Arequipa, Peru.
The truncated appearance of Ubinas, Perú's most active volcano, is a result of a 1.4-km-wide crater at the summit.
Ticsani is a dacitic lava dome complex in the Ichuna district of Peru, about 30 km SE of Huaynaputina volcano.

Huaynaputina (whose name means "new volcano") was the source of the largest historical eruption of South America in 1600 CE. It has no prominent topographic expression and lies within a 2.5-km-wide collapse…
Tutupaca consists of two dissected volcanic edifices, of which the southern appears more youthful.

The Nevados Casiri compound volcano in Peru, also known as Paugarani, lies near the Chilean border ~25 km N of Tacora volcano.
The Taapaca volcanic complex, lying W of the main Andean chain, rises NE of the small town of Putre, the principal settlement of the northern Chilean Altiplano.
The symmetrical Volcán Parinacota is the southernmost and youngest of a pair of volcanoes forming the Nevados de Payachata group along the Chile-Bolivia border.
One of northern Chile's most active volcanoes, Volcán Guallatiri is a symmetrical ice-clad stratovolcano at the SW end of the Nevados de Quimsachata volcano group.
The symmetrical Tata Sabaya towers above the northern end of the Salar de Coipasa in the Altiplano of Bolivia.
The broad Isluga volcano lies 7 km W of the Chile/Bolivia border at the W end of a group of volcanoes extending to Tata Sabaya volcano in Bolivia.
Irruputuncu is a small stratovolcano that straddles the Chile/Bolivia border.
A 15-km-long E-W ridge forming the border between Chile and Bolivia is comprised of several stratovolcanoes with Holocene lava flows.

The symmetrical steep-sided Licancabur stratovolcano was constructed primarily during the Holocene and contains a lake in its 400-m-wide summit crater.
The Cerros de Guayaques group of N-S-trending rhyodacitic lava domes straddles the Chile-Bolivia border.

The Purico volcanic complex consists of two ignimbrite sheets, separated by a short erosional interval, that were erupted about 1.3 million years ago, along with several stratovolcanoes and lava domes that define a…
Colachi is a andesitic-dacitic stratovolcano that was constructed on an uplifted block of welded ignimbrites.
Acamarachi, a steep-sided andesitic-dacitic volcano, forms the highest peak in this part of the northern Andes.
Volcán Chiliques is a structurally simple stratovolcano located immediately south of Laguna Lejía.
Volcán Putana, also known as Jorgencal or Machuca, is part of a large, roughly N-S-trending volcanic complex that covers an area of 600 km2.

Two intersecting volcanic chains, the Cordón de Puntas Negras and Cordón Chalviri, trend roughly SE from Chiliques volcano to Volcán Puntas Negras stratovolcano and SW from there to Cerro Tuyajto, respectively.
Volcán Miñiques is a large basaltic andesite to dacitic volcanic complex S of Laguna Miscanti and Laguna Miñiques.
The Cerro Tujle maar (also known as Cerro Tucle or Cerro Tugle) in the Cordón de Tujle has a 60-m-deep crater (de Silva and Francis, 1991).
Caichinque is a relatively small Pleistocene-Holocene volcanic complex that forms a topographic high dividing Salar Capur from Salar Talar.
Two small eruptive vents that produced lava flows lie about 3 km apart in the Callejón de Tilocálar area.
Cerro Pular on the NE end and Cerro Pajonales on the SW form a 12-km-long volcanic ridge NE of Socompa volcano that is mostly pre-Holocene, but may have experienced some more recent activity.

The basaltic andesite La Negrillar cone and lava flow complex (also known as Aguas Perdidas) covers a roughly 50 km2 area along the SW margin of the Atacama basin about 35 km WNW of Socompa volcano between the small…
Straddling the Chile-Argentina border, Volcán Socompa is a massive dacitic stratovolcano that lies immediately north of the only railway line between the two countries.
Láscar is the most active volcano of the northern Chilean Andes.
Cerro Escorial, a small andesitic-dacitic stratovolcano, has young-looking lava flows and a well-preserved crater.
The world's highest historically active volcano, Llullaillaco sits astride the Chile-Argentina border.
Cordón del Azufre is a small volcanic complex straddling the Chile-Argentina border.
Cerro Bayo is a complex volcano of partial Holocene age located along the Chile-Argentina border.
The Sierra Nevada volcanic complex, located in one of the most inaccessible parts of the Central Andes, covers an area of about 225 km2 astride the Chile-Argentina border.
The Falso Azufre volcanic complex is a 15-km-long, E-W trending group of overlapping craters, lava domes, and composite cones extending from Chile into Argentina.
Nevado de Incahuasi is a complex volcanic massif that straddles the Chile-Argentina border ENE of Nevados Ojos del Salado volcano.
The NNW-trending edifice of 5706-m-high Lastarria volcano along the Chile-Argentina border contains five nested summit craters.
El Solo is large stratovolcano composed of nine eruptive centers located west of Nevados del Ojos de Salado and SE of Tres Cruces volcano.
The world's highest active volcano, Nevados Ojos del Salado, rises to 6,879 m along the Chile-Argentina border.
Aracar is a steep-sided stratovolcano with a youthful-looking summit crater 1-1.5 km in diameter that contains a small lake.

An isolated basaltic andesite cinder cone was constructed on top of Miocene ignimbrites and lava flows between the Corrida de Cori range on the Chile/Argentina border and the Salar Río Grande in Argentina.
The compound volcano of Cerro el Cóndor, one of the few large stratovolcanoes located wholly in Argentina, lies within a 2.5-km-wide caldera.
The symmetrical Cerro Peinado stratovolcano in Argentina is the source of well-preserved Holocene lava flows from summit and flank vents (de Silva and Francis, 1991).
The Cerro Blanco volcanic complex contains the 5-km-diameter Cerro Blanco (or Robledo) caldera in NW Argentina, 80 km SW of the Cerro Galán caldera.
This massive volcanic complex is the world's third highest active volcano, but remains largely unknown.
The triangular Rapa Nui (also known as Isla de Pascua, or Easter Island), is renowned for its dramatic megalithic statues of hand-carved basalt.

Palomo is a small stratovolcano that is somewhat dissected by glaciers.
The 30 x 45 km Caldera del Atuel complex, ~30 km NW-SE and 45 km NE-SW, lies just east of the Argentina-Chile border and 18 km SSW of the rim of the Pleistocene Diamante caldera.
The Risco Plateado volcanic complex lies about 10 km S of the Caldera del Atuel and consists of a stratovolcano cut by a 4-km-wide caldera.
Volcán San José lies along the Chile-Argentina border at the southern end of a volcano group that includes the Pleistocene volcanoes of Marmolejo and Espíritu Santo.
Tinguiririca is composed of at least seven Holocene scoria cones W of the Chile-Argentina border constructed along a NNE-SSW fissure over an eroded Pleistocene stratovolcano.
